title: Pay With the Fewest Banknotes

concept.title: Take the biggest note that still fits, again and again
body: A country has banknotes of the values `2000, 500, 200, 100, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1`, and any number of notes of each value. To pay an amount you may give any notes that add up to **exactly** that amount. What is the smallest number of notes? For `2896` the answer is 9: `2000 + 500 + 200 + 100 + 50 + 20 + 20 + 5 + 1`, which has 9 notes (no combination uses fewer).

A *greedy* algorithm makes the choice that looks best **right now** and never looks back: take the **largest note that does not exceed the remaining amount**, subtract it, and repeat. It does not look at the future, so it is fast, and for this particular set of values it is also **correct** (each value is at least about twice the one below it and the set has no tricky gaps). For a note value `v` we can take `remaining // v` notes at once and continue with `remaining % v`.

body.code:
NOTES = [2000, 500, 200, 100, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1]
for amount in amounts:
    count = 0
    for v in NOTES:                     # from the largest to the smallest
        count += amount // v
        amount %= v
    print(count)

body: Greedy is **not** always right. With the values `1, 3, 4` and the amount 6, greedy takes `4 + 1 + 1` (3 notes), but `3 + 3` uses only 2. Whenever you use a greedy method you should have a reason why the first choice cannot hurt. Here the reason is that the values divide the tail of the amount cleanly; for general coin sets the dynamic programming solution is needed. The work is O(q * 10).

statement: Banknotes of the values 2000, 500, 200, 100, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2 and 1 are available without limit. For each of the `q` amounts, print the smallest number of notes that add up to exactly that amount.
inputFormat: The first line has `q`: the number of questions.
The second line has `q` numbers: the amounts to pay.
outputFormat: Print `q` numbers on one line, separated by spaces: the answers in the order of the questions.
hints: Take as many of the largest note as fit, then continue with the remainder.
For a note value v use amount // v and amount % v.
Go through the values from the largest to the smallest.

explanation: For each amount the largest note is taken as many times as it fits, then the next note on the remainder, and so on down to 1; for this set of values the greedy choice gives the fewest notes.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

q = int(input())
amounts = list(map(int, input().split()))

NOTES = [2000, 500, 200, 100, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1]
out = []
for amount in amounts:
    count = 0
    for v in NOTES:
        count += amount // v
        amount %= v
    out.append(count)
print(*out)
